name: HIAS: refugee resettlement and legal services in the US
beneficiaries_note: Our build: refugees, asylum seekers and other immigrants served in the US (resettlement and legal services).
summary: HIAS spent $58.7 million of its own money in the US in the year to September 2025 on refugee resettlement through about 30 local partner agencies, integration and social services, and immigration legal services for 1,433 clients, helped by $18.7 million of pro bono lawyers' time that we count as their contribution, not HIAS's cost. Resettlement is valued as the money and goods clients receive and a short head start in work, on the site's log-income scale at newly arrived refugees' consumption; legal help as the extra chance a represented asylum seeker wins the right to stay, their consumption and their remittances home against their country of origin's over the years they stay, and the deaths a removal risks. It comes to about 0.003 years of healthy life per $1,000, low because the money goes to people in the US, where a dollar is a small gain on the log scale, and because before the January 2025 suspension another agency would have resettled most of the same refugees with the same federal money; legal services give about three-fifths of it. The result is mostly uncertainty (the model's own ranges span over a thousandfold); both branches are discounted for missing data (no controlled measure of HIAS's own results), and the biggest uncertainties are that discount, what would have happened anyway, and how many losing clients would actually be removed.

rows.label: People served by resettlement, integration and social services in fiscal 2025 (legal clients apart)
rows.explainer: HIAS counts 13,400 refugees, asylum seekers and immigrants supported by its US programming in calendar 2025, legal clients included (annual report PDF p. 9), and 1,725 to 2,213 resettled in 2025 (annual report PDF p. 4; Form 990 Schedule O); in calendar 2024 it resettled 12,000 (2024 annual report). The fiscal year starts in October 2024, before admissions were suspended in January 2025, so it covers more arrivals than the calendar year (Schedule I lists about 3,400 Reception and Placement recipients in fiscal 2025), which roughly offsets taking out the 1,433 legal clients: 13,500 (9,000-28,000). Our judgment, anchored on the 13,400.

rows.label: People reached
Cost per person reached
rows.explainer: Context: the Reception and Placement grant paid $2,075 per refugee for the first months in fiscal 2017 (Congressional Research Service R44878), but most of the people served here are past those months.

rows.label: Average US consumption per person by the household survey
rows.explainer: The site's US figure (Consumer Expenditure Survey 2024).

rows.label: The people served's consumption per person, as a share of the US average
rows.explainer: Newly arrived refugees and asylum seekers live on resettlement cash, public benefits and first entry-level wages. Anchored on the poorest fifth's spending, 45% of the average per household (@united_states.ce_lowest_quintile_vs_all_2024), and below it in the first year: 35% (25-50%). Our judgment.

rows.label: The people served's consumption per person
Share of the resettlement spending that reaches clients as money or goods
rows.explainer: From the funding streams: HIAS's own direct assistance to individuals in the US was about $2.9 million (Form 990 Schedule I Part III: Reception and Placement 1,574 and 1,790 recipients, $0.28 million and $0.53 million; housing for 1,116 families separated at the border, $1.38 million), 5% of the $55 million; the local partners pass on about half of each Reception and Placement grant as rent, furniture, food and pocket money ($1,125 of $2,075 per refugee in fiscal 2017: Congressional Research Service R44878) and some cash from refugee cash and matching-grant funds, while most of their $43.9 million pays case managers, employment and social-service staff, valued in the employment row below. 20% (10-35%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Money and goods received per person served (US$)
ln(consumption) gain per person from the money and goods
rows.explainer: One year's gain on the site's log-income scale at the clients' own consumption.

rows.label: Earnings gain from employment services, as a share of consumption, a year
rows.explainer: Case managers and job developers find first jobs sooner and help with credentials and English. No controlled evaluation of US resettlement employment services exists; the Matching Grant programme reports most families self-sufficient at six months without a control group. A first job a month or two sooner and a slightly better match is a few per cent of a year's consumption: 3% (0-8%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Years the head start in work lasts
rows.explainer: Not a lifelong income gain: a head start in finding work fades as the unhelped catch up: about a year (half a year to three). Our judgment.

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per person from employment help, discounted
ln(consumption) gain per person served (resettlement)
Share of legal clients whose case decides whether they may stay
rows.explainer: HIAS's legal programme takes asylum applications and defence against removal, and also family reunification petitions, green cards and work permits (Form 990 Schedule O; annual report PDF pp. 9-10). Half (30-70%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Asylum grant rate without a lawyer (immigration courts)

source.title: TRAC, Syracuse University: asylum decisions, fiscal 2022
source.quote: Grant rates were only 18% for those who were unrepresented, but more than two and a half times higher for represented cases.

rows.explainer: The national rate for unrepresented asylum seekers in immigration court, fiscal 2022; grant rates swing between years and administrations (they fell after 2024), so 18% (12-25%).

rows.label: Grant rate with a lawyer, as a multiple of the rate without

source.title: TRAC, Syracuse University: asylum decisions, fiscal 2022
source.quote: Grant rates were only 18% for those who were unrepresented, but more than two and a half times higher for represented cases.

rows.explainer: 'More than two and a half times': 2.6 (2.5-3.0). A correlation: stronger cases find lawyers more easily, which evidence_adj discounts. Eagly and Shafer's national study of 1.2 million removal cases found represented immigrants five and a half times as likely to obtain relief (University of Pennsylvania Law Review, 2015), also uncontrolled.

rows.label: Extra chance of winning the right to stay with representation
Chance a client who loses is actually removed
rows.explainer: Reference class: removals against final removal orders. ICE counted 1,445,549 people on its non-detained docket with final removal orders in November 2024 (ICE figures reported by Fox News, https://www.foxnews.com/politics/new-data-reveals-america-has-tens-thousands-noncitizens-from-us-adversary-deportation-orders, about 55% of them executable) against 271,484 removals in fiscal 2024 (ICE annual report, https://www.ice.gov/doclib/eoy/iceAnnualReportFY2024.pdf), a quarter to a third a year of the roughly 800,000 executable orders, so many who lost stayed for years; since 2025 removals, detention and 'third-country' deportations have risen sharply (annual report PDF p. 5) and asylum seekers with known addresses are the easiest to find. 40% (15-70%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Consumption per person, Honduras (PPP dollars, 2024)
rows.explainer: The site's household-survey consumption per person (World Bank PIP mean, 2021 PPP dollars a day, × 365, US prices to 2024, real growth to 2024), in purchasing-power dollars, so it compares directly with US consumption.

rows.label: Consumption per person, Kenya (PPP dollars, 2024)
rows.explainer: The site's household-survey consumption per person (World Bank PIP mean, 2021 PPP dollars a day, × 365, US prices to 2024, real growth to 2024), in purchasing-power dollars, so it compares directly with US consumption.

rows.label: Consumption per person, Peru (PPP dollars, 2024)
rows.explainer: The site's household-survey consumption per person (World Bank PIP mean, 2021 PPP dollars a day, × 365, US prices to 2024, real growth to 2024), in purchasing-power dollars, so it compares directly with US consumption.

rows.label: Share of legal clients from Latin America
rows.explainer: Most asylum seekers in US immigration courts are from Latin America; HIAS's New York and Silver Spring clients include many Africans (Cameroon in the annual report's story) and Afghans. 55% (35-75%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Of the Latin American clients, share from Central America
rows.explainer: Honduras, Guatemala and El Salvador are among the largest asylum nationalities in US courts, with Venezuela, Colombia and Ecuador from South America. Half (30-75%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Consumption per person in the clients' countries of origin (PPP dollars)
rows.formula: leg_latam_share * (leg_central_america_share * cons_ppp_hnd + (1 - leg_central_america_share) * cons_ppp_per) + (1 - leg_latam_share) * cons_ppp_ken
rows.explainer: Honduras stands in for Central America, Peru for South America, Kenya for Africa and Asia (a richer stand-in than Cameroon or Afghanistan, so the gain is if anything understated).

rows.label: Clients' consumption over the years they stay, as a share of the US average
rows.explainer: Refugees' and asylees' earnings rise steeply in their first decade in the US, from well below to near the poorest fifth's and then the second fifth's level (@united_states.ce_lowest_quintile_vs_all_2024 0.45 per household, higher per person; @united_states.ce_second_quintile_vs_all_2024 for the next fifth). Averaged over 20 years: 60% (40-80%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Clients' consumption per person over the years they stay (US$)
Share of their consumption that clients send home
rows.explainer: Latin American migrants in the US send money home about 13 times a year (Inter-American Dialogue, https://thedialogue.org/press-release/remittances-to-latin-america-and-the-caribbean-grew-over-8-in-2017-according-to-new-research-by-the-inter-american-dialogue), around $300 each time for the median Mexican sender (NPR, https://www.npr.org/sections/goatsandsoda/2017/02/10/514172676/mexicans-in-the-u-s-are-sending-home-more-money-than-ever), roughly a tenth of a low-wage income; newly arrived asylum seekers earn and send less at first. 6% (2-12%) of consumption. Our judgment.

rows.label: People in the family a remittance supports
rows.explainer: The site's household size for Honduras, standing in for the countries of origin.

rows.label: Years until a lost case would end in removal
rows.explainer: The average wait in the immigration courts was 1,424 days, about 3.9 years, in March 2024 (TRAC, reported at https://gigafact.org/fact-briefs/is-the-waiting-period-for-an-immigration-asylum-hearing-six-to-eight-years); courts sped up decisions in 2025, and removal follows the final order: 3 years (1-5). Our judgment.

rows.label: Years in the US gained by a client who wins and would otherwise have been removed
rows.explainer: Most asylum seekers are young adults with decades ahead; some would later regularise another way or leave. 20 years (8-40). Our judgment.

rows.label: ln(consumption) value of staying rather than being removed, discounted from the removal
rows.formula: (ln(leg_cons_stayed * (1 - leg_remit_share) / leg_cons_origin) + origin_household_size * ln(1 + leg_remit_share * leg_cons_stayed / (leg_cons_origin * origin_household_size))) * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, leg_years_stayed) * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ (0 - leg_wait_years)
rows.explainer: The site's log-income scale at each person's own consumption: the US level the client lives at, less what they send home, against their country of origin, and the family at home's gain from the remittances, each year they stay, counted from when a removal would have come.

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per legal client
Chance a removed asylum seeker is killed in the years after return
rows.explainer: Human Rights Watch documented 138 Salvadorans killed after deportation from the US between 2013 and 2019, a likely undercount, against roughly 100,000 deported to El Salvador in those years ('Deported to Danger', 2020): over 0.1%. Asylum seekers fleeing persecution face more than deportees on average: 0.3% (0.05-1%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Deaths averted per legal client
rows.explainer: Discounted from when a removal would have come.

rows.label: Life satisfaction gained by other legal clients (points, 0-10) a year
rows.explainer: The other half: families reunited and green cards won, which ease worry and separation (work permits' income is a side-effect row). Studies of family separation among refugees find large distress; one point-year of life satisfaction is about the gap a reunion closes in the worst cases. A tenth of a point (0-0.3) averaged over all such clients, most of whose cases would succeed anyway or bring smaller relief. Our judgment.

rows.label: Years the other clients' gain lasts
rows.explainer: A reunion or a status lasts, but the gain over the alternative (a later success without help) fades: two years (1-4). Our judgment.

rows.label: WELLBYs per legal client, discounted
Life satisfaction gained per person per year, all people reached (reading only)
rows.explainer: Outcome summary for reading only: the legal branch's other clients, spread over everyone reached.

rows.label: WELLBYs per person reached (reading only)
rows.explainer: Summary for reading only: the legal branch's WELLBYs spread over everyone reached.

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per person reached (reading only)
rows.explainer: Summary for reading only: both branches' log-income gains over everyone reached.

rows.label: Deaths averted per person reached (reading only)
rows.explainer: Summary for reading only: the legal branch's deaths averted over everyone reached.

rows.label: Illness averted per person reached, in DALYs
rows.explainer: Zero: no health effect is modelled apart from deaths; health insurance enrolment and mental-health referrals are in the unmodelled shares.

rows.label: Share of the deaths averted under five
rows.explainer: Removed with a parent: children are a small share of HIAS's adult asylum clients' households removed. 3% (0-10%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Of those five or older, share aged 5 to 14
rows.explainer: Older children removed with their families: 7% (2-15%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Of those 15 or older, share aged 15 to 49
rows.explainer: Asylum seekers killed after return are mostly young adults (Human Rights Watch's cases): 90% (75-97%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: GiveWell's moral weights by age band, times your value of a life.

rows.label: Resettlement: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: The money and goods are counted at their value, but the employment gain has no controlled evidence and some of the goods (furniture, household items) are worth less to clients than their cost. 0.6 (0.4-0.85), about as for the employment and case-management branches of the site's other domestic-services models. Our judgment.

rows.label: Share of the year's resettlement spending before the January 2025 suspension
rows.explainer: Federal awards were suspended on 24 January 2025 (statements note 1), four of the fiscal year's twelve months in: four months at fiscal 2024's $91.1 million a year is $30.4 million of the year's $80.4 million (Exhibit B), 38%, a little more if spending wound down after the suspension. 40% (30-60%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Resettlement before the suspension: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Reference class: the national agencies split arrivals by capacity; without HIAS another agency would have taken its cases with the same federal money, a little less well where HIAS's partners have local ties. 20% (5-40%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Resettlement after the suspension: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: After January 2025, HIAS's private money kept case management and emergency help going for refugees already here whom federal programmes had dropped; other agencies were cutting too. 60% (30-85%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Resettlement: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: The two periods weighted by their share of the spending.

rows.label: Resettlement: HIAS's share of the resources
rows.explainer: The local partners add their own fundraising, volunteers and Welcome Circles of community sponsors (117 Afghan SIV holders assisted: annual report PDF p. 9). 75% (50-90%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Legal services: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: The represented-versus-unrepresented gap is a correlation: lawyers pick stronger cases and stronger applicants find lawyers. Studies that compare like cases keep a large effect (Eagly and Shafer control for case traits and still find much higher odds), so about half of the raw gap: 0.5 (0.3-0.75). Our judgment.

rows.label: Legal services: share of clients who would not have found another lawyer
rows.explainer: About half of people in removal proceedings find counsel (Eagly, Shafer and Moulton, 2025: 52%); HIAS takes clients who can't pay. 60% (35-85%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Hours of donated legal services

source.title: HIAS, 2025 Annual Report
source.quote: 18,000 hours of donated legal services by pro bono partners, valued at over $18.6 million

rows.explainer: Lawyers from law firms working HIAS's cases, calendar 2025.

rows.label: Value of a donated lawyer's hour, for the credit share
rows.explainer: Convention 2 values volunteers' time at the local wage. A US lawyer's median pay is about $73 an hour (BLS, 2024), about $100-120 with benefits; the accounts' $1,040 an hour is the firms' billing rate. $120 ($70-300). Our judgment.

rows.label: Legal services: HIAS's share of the resources
rows.explainer: Convention 2: HIAS's own legal spending, with overhead, over that plus the pro bono lawyers' time at their wage.

rows.label: Delivery adjustment
rows.explainer: HIAS's counts are its own; some clients served get only a consultation or drop out. 0.9 (0.75-1). Our judgment.

rows.label: Resettlement: leverage and funging
rows.explainer: Government grants paid for most of the resettlement work ($74 million of HIAS's $155 million revenue, Exhibit B) until January 2025; a private dollar partly replaces cut federal money that may be restored by the courts. 0.95 (0.8-1.05). Our judgment.

rows.label: Legal services: leverage and funging
rows.explainer: The legal programme runs on private money and pro bono time; a donation neither displaces nor draws in other money much. 1 (0.9-1.05). Our judgment.

rows.label: Resettlement: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin (Convention 12): the reach is a judgment around HIAS's calendar-year count and the employment gain has no controlled measure, so the branch reads the shared missing-data slider.

rows.label: Legal services: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin: HIAS counts its legal clients, but the effect of its representation is from national, uncontrolled comparisons, not a measure of its own cases' outcomes, so the branch reads the shared missing-data slider.

rows.formula: leg_evidence_adj * leg_counterfactual_adj * leg_attribution_share * implementation_adj * leg_leverage_funging_adj * leg_missing_data_adj

rows.label: Unmodelled: social support and integration
rows.explainer: Case management, English classes, school enrolment and community sponsors help people settle and feel less alone, beyond money: +5% (0 to +15%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Unmodelled: health insurance enrolment and mental-health referrals
rows.explainer: Clients are enrolled in Medicaid and refugee medical assistance and referred for trauma care: +3% (0 to +10%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Unmodelled: effects on host communities
rows.explainer: Refugees' work and taxes in the towns that receive them (positive), against some pressure on local services (negative): +1% (-2% to +5%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Unmodelled: collecting refugees' travel loans
rows.explainer: HIAS collects refugees' flight loans for the IOM and keeps 25% (statements p. 12): a burden on new arrivals, softened by its credit-building advice. -0.5% (-2% to 0). Our judgment.

rows.label: Unmodelled: legal clients' work permits won sooner
rows.explainer: Help with work authorisation lets clients earn sooner, beyond the right to stay: +2% of the legal branch (0 to +6%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Unmodelled: social services for legal clients
rows.explainer: HIAS's social services team gives legal clients case management, food and transport help and referrals (annual report PDF p. 10): +3% of the legal branch (0 to +8%). Our judgment.
